rashi:a1.1: We assess him once: and he gives twice the amount.
rashi:a3.1: They assessed him on his own: without any need, just in passing as talk, and ten were present; what is the halakha?
tosafot:a3.1: They assessed him on his own, what is the halakha? Do we say etc.: this dilemma does not follow with “if you say” from the one before it, like the earlier ones; he could have asked it on its own, but he wanted to combine it with the other dilemmas.
gershom:a1.1: They assessed him on his own: when he had not said, “My assessment is incumbent upon me.”
rashi:a4.1: Resolve from this: [from] our mishna, one of these dilemmas.
rashi:a4.2: As there is no monetary value for the dead: and from the outset we do not know how much he was worth.
gershom:a2.1: As there is no monetary value for the dead: for once he has died, a person cannot know how much he was worth when he was alive.
rashi:a5.1: Isn’t he standing assessed: for there is no person who is not worth four zuz.
gershom:a3.1: Is there a man who is not worth four zuz while alive? So it is as though he had been assessed, and the heirs should give [his] assessment.
rashi:a6.1: He has not entered into an assessment: he was never assessed; only now would we assess him, and we require an assessment.
gershom:a4.1: When they assessed him on his own, he entered into an assessment: and they examined carefully how much he was worth.
gershom:a5.1: “My assessment is incumbent upon me,” and he died: he never entered into a complete assessment in the first place; therefore the heirs do not give.
rashi:a7.1: Mishna. My valuation is incumbent upon me: it is a fixed sum, so the heirs give it.
rashi:a7.2: As there is no monetary value for the dead: and as for what is taught in Bava Kamma (27a) [about an ox that killed], “Then he shall give the ransom of his life” — the value of the one damaged — there the reason is that from the moment it did the damage, payment fell upon him as of the time of the damage, and at the time it damaged him he was alive. But with “My assessment is incumbent upon me,” he vows only what the court will assess him at, and he never came to that, since he died; [so] the heirs do not give.
tosafot:a7.1: “My assessment is incumbent upon me,” and he died, the heirs do not give, as there is no monetary value [for the dead] etc.: and as for what is taught in Bava Kamma (27a), “Then he shall give the ransom of his life,” the value of the one damaged, meaning that they assess him after his death at what he was worth while alive: that is a decree of Scripture. But here he vows only the value the court will assess him at, and he never came to an assessment, since he died; [so] the heirs do not give his value.
rashi:a8.1: He gives the valuation of his entire self: “a valuation of living people [nefashot]” is written.
rashi:a9.1: The valuation of half of me is incumbent upon me: this is like “the valuation of my head” and “the valuation of my liver,” since it is something on which life depends.
rashi:a9.2: The assessment of half of me is incumbent upon me, he gives the assessment of his entire self: for it is taught in the chapter Hassag Yad (above, Arakhin 18a): you have juxtaposed assessments to valuations, to judge [a limb] by its importance.
rashi:a11.1: Gemara. On a domesticated animal: if he said, “The assessment of my animal is incumbent upon me.” But a valuation applies only to a person.
tosafot:a11.1: The Sages taught: more stringent with regard to vows than with regard to valuations etc.: it is puzzling: why does the Gemara not object to our mishna, which teaches “this is a stringency of vows over valuations” [so Tosafot; our mishna opens with the stringency of valuations over vows]: this stringency, and no more? But there are these of the baraita! The Gemara asks that way in Bava Metzia, chapter HaZahav (57b), about “this is a stringency of consecrated property over ordinary property,” objecting: “this stringency, and no more? There are many!” Let us ask the same here. One can answer that there, finding a stringency of consecrated property over ordinary property is no novelty, since it is only logical to be stricter with consecrated property than with ordinary property; that is why the Talmud wonders, “this stringency and no more? There are many.” But here, where it is a novelty to be stricter with vows than with valuations, it is not fitting to object, “this stringency and no more?”, since the tanna taught some and left some out.
rashi:a11.2: And they are not judged by affordability: if he said, “My assessment is incumbent upon me,” and he cannot afford it, he gives all of it when he is able.
tosafot:a11.2: And they are not judged by affordability, as valuations are: this is difficult, for above (Arakhin 18a) we juxtaposed assessments to valuations, [as in] “a pearl for the poor,” and there is no juxtaposition by halves [that is, a juxtaposition should apply in every respect]. One can say there is a single exclusion: regarding valuations it is written “the priest shall valuate him [ya’arikhenu],” which implies him and not another; so with valuations one is judged by affordability, “as the priest shall valuate him,” and not with vows.
gershom:a6.1: And is not judged by affordability: rather he gives all that he has, and gives again when he has more.
rashi:a13.1: Conclude from this that a loan by oral agreement etc.: and this is a dispute in several places.
gershom:a7.1: Here it is different, as it is a loan written in the Torah: since he said “My valuation is incumbent upon me,” it is already written in the Torah how much he must give.
rashi:a14.1: Conclude from this that a loan written [in the Torah] etc.: and this is a dispute in tractate Bekhorot, in the chapter Yesh Bekhor LaNaḥala (49b).
rashi:a14.2: Where he stood in judgment: and they obligated him before his death, so that it is like a loan with a document.
gershom:a8.1: Where he stood in judgment: and they obligated him to give; and whatever stands to be collected is considered as collected.
rashi:a15.1: Why should the heirs not give: after all, the court has assessed him.
rashi:a15.2: It lacks an assessment: they obligated him to pay but did not manage to assess him before he died.
gershom:a9.1: It lacks an assessment: where he stood in judgment and they did not assess him, and he died. [The text runs on: “He has not said anything.”]
gershom:a10.1: [A note in the printed text: it seems something is missing here, and it should read:] “The valuation of my hand and the valuation of my foot is incumbent upon me”: he has not said anything, since life does not depend on it. And he gives its assessment: of the hand, that is, etc., since life does not depend on it.
rashi:a17.1: He has not said anything, according to the Rabbis: who say in the first chapter (above, Arakhin 5a) that a person utters words for naught.
rashi:a17.2: He gives its assessment: and we established in the first chapter that he said it according to Rabbi Meir.
gershom:a11.1: And he gives its assessment: of the hand. That is, since a person does not utter his words for naught, and it is known that there is no valuation for a hand, he made up his mind and spoke for the sake of assessment, and he gives its assessment.
gershom:a12.1: According to Rabbi Meir, who says in our first chapter: one who valuates [an infant] less than a month old, Rabbi Meir says he gives its assessment, etc.
rashi:a19.1: But he did not say “assessment”: and therefore he should not give an assessment. [Rav Giddel] teaches us [that he does].
gershom:a13.1: He was mistaken, thinking etc.; but not “assessment”: that is, he did not intend it for the sake of assessment, and should not give its assessment. [Rav Giddel] teaches us [that he does].
gershom:a14.1: To include from the knee and above: if he said, “The valuation of my leg, from the knee and above, is incumbent upon me,” he gives the valuation of his entire self.
rashi:a25.1: A vow by your valuation: vows were juxtaposed to valuations.
gershom:a15.1: [What is the reason? “A vow by your valuation” is written; that is, whatever applies to valuations applies to assessments, which is “a vow.”]
tosafot:a26.1: To include from the knee and above: and if you ask, why does he mention the leg from the knee and above rather than any of the other eighteen tereifot [injuries from which an animal cannot survive]? One can say that this one is more of a novelty, to exclude the view of Rabbi Shimon, who says (Ḥullin 42b) that it can be cauterized and live.
tosafot:a27.1: The Sages taught: one who valuates half the valuation of a vessel, Rabbi Meir says he gives its assessment: so most books read, and it does not seem right, for if so, what does it mean just below, “half, it is not the usual way to donate”? Why should it not be usual to donate half the worth of a vessel? So the Ri holds that the reading is “one who valuates the valuation of half a vessel.” Now it works out that he says “half, it is not the usual way to donate,” because half a vessel is worth nothing; that is why he says “half, it is not the usual way to donate.”
gershom:a16.1: And the Rabbis say he has not said anything: when he valuated half a vessel; but if he valuated a whole vessel, he gives its assessment.
rashi:a27.1: No difference whether all of it, no difference whether half of it: and it teaches us half of it, and all the more so all of it; for although it is not the usual way to donate half the value of a vessel, even so he gives, and all the more so all of it.
rashi:a28.1: Even all of it as well: even if he said, “The valuation of this vessel is incumbent upon me,” he should be exempt.
rashi:a29.1: They hold like Rabbi Meir: and that is why they do not disagree about all of it.
rashi:a30.1: Rabbi Shimon exempts one who says, “I take upon myself a meal offering of barley,” in Menaḥot (103a) [the printed Rashi says “in the second chapter” of Menaḥot].
gershom:a17.1: [They hold like Rabbi Meir, who says a person does not utter his words for naught, where he donated in the manner of donors, when he valuated all of it. Half, it is not the usual way to donate; therefore he has not said anything, since they hold like Rabbi Shimon.]
rashi:a31.1: What is it? Where he stood in judgment: that is, how can the mishna that teaches “the heirs give” be explained? Necessarily where he stood in judgment before his death, as we explained the first clause; so why does it teach it again?
gershom:a18.1: What is it: one who says, “The valuation of so-and-so is incumbent upon me,” [and both the one who vowed and the object of the vow died: why should the heirs give? Where the one who valuated stood in judgment before he died.]
gershom:a19.1: That is the same: in the passage above, one said “My valuation is incumbent upon me” and died, the heirs give, and we explained it as where he stood in judgment.
rashi:b1.1: Lest you say: although the one who vowed stood in judgment before his death, since the object of the vow was not assessed in the lifetime of the one who vowed, the property of the orphans [his heirs] is not liened.
rashi:b1.2: It is a mere disclosure of the matter: to reveal how much he owes; and since the object of the vow is alive, we assess him.
gershom:b1.1: The property was liened: to the Temple.
gershom:b2.1: And the assessment: since it depends not on the one who vowed but on the object of the vow, whatever lay upon the one who vowed to pay, the court obligated him, and the heirs are obligated; and the assessment is a mere disclosure of the matter, for anyone can assess him, even someone who is not a court, and whatever any person says he was worth, [the heirs of] the one who vowed shall give. But [with one who says “My assessment is incumbent upon me”] and dies, since he himself needs to be assessed and they did not assess him, the heirs are exempt.
rashi:b2.1: Mishna. And this house is an offering: for Temple maintenance.
rashi:b2.2: And the house collapsed: before the Temple treasurer took possession of it.
gershom:b3.1: And this house is an offering: for its value.
gershom:b4.1: Exempt: from paying, since he said “this” and did not accept responsibility for it.
gershom:b5.1: But if he said “upon me”: he accepted responsibility for it, and is obligated to pay.
rashi:b3.1: Gemara. They taught only — that when he said “upon me” he must pay — where he said “the monetary value is incumbent upon me”: for if the bull is lost, the value is not lost, since he did not say “this money,” and it was not in existence.
rashi:b3.2: Upon me to bring it: to take the trouble until it is offered.
gershom:b6.1: They taught only: that he bears responsibility.
gershom:b7.1: But where he said “The monetary value of this bull is incumbent upon me”: that is, if it is stolen, I am obligated for its value.
gershom:b8.1: [He meant: it is upon me to bring it, if it exists.]
tosafot:b3.1: In brief: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Rav explains “upon me” in “this bull is upon me” as “upon me to bring it,” that is, to take the trouble until it is offered. Tosafot ask: if so, what does the first clause of the mishna, “This bull is a burnt offering … exempt from paying,” teach us, when even with “upon me” he is exempt, as Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Rav concludes? The Ri says the whole mishna, first clause and latter clause, speaks of one who said “the monetary value”: “The value of this bull is a burnt offering,” “the value of this house is an offering,” and the bull died or the house fell, he is exempt, since he did not say “upon me”; but “the value of this bull is upon me as a burnt offering,” “the value of this house is upon me as an offering,” he must pay. So it is in Rosh HaShana (6a): a vow is where he said “upon me,” a gift offering is where he said “this is”; with a vow, if it died or was stolen he bears responsibility, with a gift offering he does not. The mishna’s “this bull” teaches a novelty: although he said “this,” since he said “upon me” he bears responsibility. The Ri adds that at first sight, one who says “the value of this bull is upon me as a burnt offering” leaves the bull itself non-sacred, like one who says “the value of so-and-so’s bull is upon me,” where the bull stays non-sacred because a person cannot consecrate another’s ox. It is not like one who consecrates a male animal for its value, which Temurah (19b) says receives inherent sanctity (once sanctity of value comes upon it, inherent sanctity comes upon it too), since there he said “let this bull be consecrated for its value”; and so below in our passage, when he says “let the bull be consecrated for its value,” the bull itself is sacred. tosafot:b4.1: In brief: The baraita says “This bull is upon me as a burnt offering: the bull is consecrated, one is liable for misuse of it, and if it died or was stolen he bears responsibility.” So we do not say “he meant: upon me to bring it,” which is difficult for Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Rav; and the Gemara answers that, as with the mishna, the baraita speaks of one who said “the monetary value.” Tosafot ask: according to the explanation [of the Ri, in the previous Tosafot] that in such a case the bull itself is non-sacred, how can the baraita say the bull is consecrated? According to Rashi’s explanation here it works out, and Tosafot quote Rashi’s note on “Here too, he says ‘monetary value’” in full: that the case is “Let this bull be consecrated for its value, and its value is upon me as a burnt offering,” so the bull is sacred and he bears responsibility; and that “upon me” here refers to responsibility, not to the trouble of bringing it, since the money was not before him and he did not say “this money.” Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:b9.1: If it died or was stolen he bears responsibility for it: [since he said “upon me”], even though he did not say “monetary value.”
rashi:b5.1: Here too, he says “monetary value”: as we explain below, that he said “Let this bull be consecrated for its value, and the value is upon me as a burnt offering.” So the bull is sacred, since he said “let the bull be consecrated,” and if it died he bears responsibility, since he said “upon me.” And here one cannot say as was said above, that since he said “this” he meant to exempt himself from responsibility and “upon me” refers to the trouble of bringing it. Here, where the money was not before him and he did not say “this [money],” “upon me” certainly refers to responsibility; and when he said “this,” he meant: let this bull be sacred until I sell it and bring its value.
tosafot:b6.1: In brief: The Gemara could have objected straight from the latter clause of the baraita to the mishna as Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Rav explains it, since that clause says “the value of this [bull] is upon me as a burnt offering: the bull is non-sacred … if it died or was stolen he does not bear responsibility,” while the mishna says he must pay; but having begun its objection from the first clause, it finished it there, and the answer settles everything. A difficulty: in Ḥullin (139a), on one who consecrated a maneh for Temple maintenance and it was stolen or lost, Rabbi Yoḥanan says he bears responsibility until it reaches the treasurer, and Reish Lakish says that wherever it is, it is in the treasury of the Merciful One (“The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness”), so even with “upon me” he is not obligated; and the Gemara there objects to Reish Lakish from our mishna, “This bull is upon me as a burnt offering … he must pay.” What is the objection? Reish Lakish speaks of one who set the maneh aside, and our mishna of one who set nothing aside, since we explained the bull itself as non-sacred. It seems that passage does not accept Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Rav’s explanation that the mishna speaks of “monetary value.” So the Ri holds that in our mishna the bull itself is sacred, like one who consecrates a male animal for its value, which receives inherent sanctity. It is unlike one who takes his fellow’s bull upon himself, which does not become sacred because a person cannot consecrate another’s property (though whatever he can apply sanctity to, he does); here the bull is his own, so when he says “the value of this bull is upon me as a burnt offering,” the bull itself is sacred. Now the objection in Ḥullin works, since a sacred bull is as though he set it aside, like one who consecrated a maneh; and our passage works too, objecting from the baraita and answering that the bull is consecrated as it teaches, and so too in the mishna. A small difficulty remains: why must the first clause be explained as “let the bull be consecrated for its value,” when saying “the value of this bull is upon me” already makes the bull sacred? One must say the first clause is read as though he said “let the bull be consecrated for its value,” and the bull is sacred. Or else Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Rav’s “only where he said ‘the value of this bull is upon me’” itself means he said “let the bull be consecrated for its value, and its value as a burnt offering,” and the bull is sacred; with that the whole passage works, and so does the objection in Ḥullin from our mishna to Reish Lakish. rashi:b6.1: The bull is non-sacred: for he consecrated only the coins of the bull’s value, once it is sold.
rashi:b6.2: He does not bear responsibility for it: since it was not sold, it turns out he consecrated nothing.
rashi:b6.3: But he does bear responsibility for its value: if the bull was sold and the money became sacred and was lost, he bears responsibility for it.
gershom:b10.1: [The bull is non-sacred: since he consecrated only its value.] (He does not bear responsibility, since he spoke of the value of the bull, and once it died there is no monetary value for the dead, as we say in the mishna: “My assessment is incumbent upon me,” and he died, the heirs do not give.)
rashi:b7.1: The first clause is where he said “Let the bull be consecrated for its value”: so he bears responsibility, since sanctity of value took effect on the bull and he accepted responsibility for its value; and this “upon me” means responsibility, since it refers to the value, and the value was not before him that he could say “this.”
rashi:b7.2: The latter clause is where he said “When its value comes, let it be consecrated”: so he does not bear responsibility, for since the bull died and never came to be money, it turns out he consecrated nothing.
gershom:b11.1: The first clause is where he said “Let the bull be consecrated, upon me, for its value”: since he said “let the bull be consecrated,” the bull is sacred and one is liable for misuse of it; and since he said “for its value,” that is why it says that if it died or was stolen he bears responsibility.
gershom:b12.1: [And the latter clause is where he said “When its value comes, let it be consecrated,” when it is sold; since he did not say “let the bull be consecrated,” it is not consecrated, and he does not bear responsibility.]
gershom:b13.1: But a person cannot consecrate something that has not come into the world: so how do these coins become sacred when they come?
rashi:b8.1: It is Rabbi Meir: as it is taught: “You are betrothed to me after I convert,” “after you convert,” etc.; Rabbi Meir says she is betrothed.
gershom:b14.1: It is Rabbi Meir: [who says a person can consecrate something that has not come into the world], in tractate Kiddushin.
rashi:b10.1: And some teach it: this statement of Rav Yehuda, and of Abaye and of Rami bar Ḥama.
rashi:b10.2: Even though a priest confirmed it: saying it is impure and stands to be dismantled. As long as he has not dismantled it, the landlord says to the renter, “That which is yours is before you,” and I will not rent you another house, since the house I rented you is standing.
rashi:b10.3: He dismantled it: the priest did; the landlord must provide the renter with another house, for this came about through the landlord’s fortune, since he is suspected of theft or of stinginess.
tosafot:b10.1: In brief: The Ri says this shows that a confirmed leprous house is permitted for benefit, which is why the landlord can say “that which is yours is before you,” as in the mishna in Bava Metzia, chapter HaUmanin (78a): one who hired a donkey and it went blind or was seized for royal service, [the owner] says “that which is yours is before you.” Were a confirmed house forbidden for benefit, it would be like a donkey that died or broke a leg, where the mishna there says he must provide another donkey. But my teacher found this difficult: Torat Kohanim says of garments, “a malignant [mam’eret] leprosy,” give it a curse [me’era], that one may not benefit from it, which implies it is forbidden for benefit. So too in Yevamot, chapter Mitzvat Ḥalitza (103b), Rav Pappa says in the name of Rava: with a quarantined sandal she should not perform ḥalitza, but if she did, her ḥalitza is valid; with a confirmed sandal she should not, and if she did, her ḥalitza is invalid. Rashi there explains that with a quarantined sandal she should not do it at the outset, by decree because of a confirmed one, yet it is valid because mitzvot were not given for benefit; so a confirmed sandal is forbidden for benefit. One must therefore say that it is indeed forbidden for benefit, and “that which is yours is before you” is where he said “this house”: since it is still standing he need not provide another house, but he loses his rent, as with a donkey that died or broke a leg, where it says there he must provide another donkey, and Rashi there adds, or lose his fee. gershom:b15.1: And it became afflicted: in the renter’s possession; even though the priest confirmed it and it is forbidden for benefit.
gershom:b16.1: [A note in the printed text: it seems it should read] the landlord says to the renter, “That which is yours is before you,” what you rented. [Even a landlord to a renter; for he cannot say “That which is yours is before you” about what he sold.]
gershom:b17.1: He dismantled it: the priest did.
